statement: Lecture 3 agenda: foundation for ID generation, monotonically increasing IDs, central ID generation service, database ticket servers, Twitter's idea, Instagram improving it.
detail: Title slide: SYSTEM DESIGN MASTERCLASS - Distributed ID Generators.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Agenda : - Foundation for ID generation - Monotonically increasing IDs - Central ID generation service - Database Ticket Servers - Twitter's Insane Idea ...

statement: An ID gives uniqueness to an object, row, document or event.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ID : Uniqueness to an object / row / document / event

statement: Problem statement: assign a globally unique ID to anything, by writing a function that returns something unique every time it is invoked.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Assign a globally unique ID to "anything" Write a function that spits out something unique everytime it is invoked !

statement: The ID function being designed is part of the application logic, not a central service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * The function we are writing is part of the application logic and NOT a central service

statement: Time is unique through time because it always moves forward.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, what is unique throught time ? TIME -> always moves forward

statement: First attempt: get_id() returns the current epoch milliseconds; since time moves forward every call seems unique.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: func get_id() { return get_epoch_ms(); } Every time the function invoked the time would have moved forward & hence it seems unique !

statement: Epoch-ms IDs only work when there is one machine and the code is never invoked twice within the same millisecond.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The ID generation logic works fine when there is just one machine and the code is not invoked twice within one ms.

statement: With multiple machines, calls at the same time on two machines produce the same ID (collision).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Function invoked at the same time on two machines will generate the same ID ... collision !!

statement: Fix: prepend the machine id to the time, so m1 and m2 at t=1729 get m1-1729 and m2-1729; get_id returns concat(machine_id, get_epoch_ms()).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We prepend machine id to time... return concat ( machine_id, get_epoch_ms() ); id : m1-1729 m2-1729

statement: Threads: the function can be invoked by two threads of the same program at the same time, so machine id + time can still collide.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if the program has threads ? Function can be invoked by two threads at the same time

statement: Two options for threads: add thread_id as a differentiator, or add a counter that resets every few minutes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1. Add thread_id as a differentiator 2. Add counter that resek every few minutes

statement: ID = concat(machine_id, thread_id, get_epoch_ms()), e.g. m1-t1-1729, m1-t2-1729, m2-t1-1729.
detail: Board's last example reads m2 - t3 - 1729, likely a slip for t2.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: return concat( machine_id, thread_id, get_epoch_ms() ); id: m1 - t1 - 1729 m2 - t1 - 1729 m1 - t2 - 1729

statement: Static counter: int counter = 0; ID = concat(machine_id, get_epoch_ms(), counter++), e.g. m1-1729-01, m1-1729-02, m1-1729-03.
detail: Heading spelled 'concaknating' (concatenating). Third right-hand ID reads m3 - 1730 - 03, likely a slip for m2.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: concaknating static counter int counter =0; return concat( machine_id, get_epoch_ms(), counter ++ ); m1 - 1729 - 01

statement: If we already have a static counter, the time part is redundant, so it is dropped: IDs become m1-01, m1-02, m1-03.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if we already have static counter , then time is redundant...

statement: A static counter lives in memory and is volatile: if the machine dies or the process restarts, the counter starts again from 0 and regenerates the same IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Static counter is in memory ... volatile if machine dies, or process rebooks - counter starts again from 0 - regenerates the same IDs

statement: Fix for fault tolerance: store the counter to disk (non-volatile) on every increment; on start, counter = load().
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Store counter to disk (non-volatile) -> Fault Tolerance Everytime counter++ , we store it to the disk int counter = load();

statement: Saving the counter on every call means a disk I/O on every ID invocation.
detail: Right-hand text is cut off by the participant tiles ('a', 'eve').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: save_counter(); ---> Disk I/o We are making a Disk I/o upon every invocation

statement: Optimisation: save the counter only every N (e.g. 1000) increments (flush frequency); on start load the saved value and add the flush frequency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Instead of doing it every time, let's save counter every 10.. int counter = load() + 1000; ---> Flush frequency if (counter % 1000 ...

statement: Flush-every-3 example: m1-01..m1-08 with flushes at 03 and 06 and a crash at 08; on disk is 06, so the safe restart value is 06 + 3 + 1 = m1-10.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Say, disk flush happens every 3 values ... On disk values 03 06 New starting value (safe) is = 06 + 3 + 1 ...

statement: Monotonically increasing IDs help in conflict resolution, e.g. deciding who came first (whether thread T1 wrote before T2).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if we only want monotonically increasing IDs ? Why? Monotonically increasing IDs helps in conflict resolution eg: who came first

statement: Example: a = 10, thread T1 sets a = 20 and thread T2 sets a = 30; how can we say T1 came before T2?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: a = 10 T1 a = 20 T2 a = 30 How can we say that T1 came before T2 ?

statement: For ordering, put time first: get_id returns concat(get_time_ms(), machine_id) - time then machine instead of machine then time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: return concat( get_time_ms(), machine_id ); Instead of machine_time, we now put time - machine

statement: All ID generation algorithms put time on the left-hand side for sortability.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * All ID generation algorithms have time on LHS "sortability"

statement: The left part is the most significant: it makes sorting simple and decides the order; a conflict in the first half is broken by the second half (tie breaking).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: LHS : Most significant part Makes sorting simple Conflict in the first half ↳ Tie breaking in the second

statement: Example IDs with time (epoch ms) as the first 4 digits and a counter/machine part after: 1729 0001, 1729 0002, 1730 0001, 1730 0002, 1730 0003, 1731 0001.
speaker: teacher

statement: Time-first IDs still do not guarantee monotonicity because clocks across machines can go out of sync.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Although a good solution, but it still does not guarantee Monotonicity ! Because clocks across machines can go out of sync

statement: Four machines 2, 4, 7, 9 with clocks 23, 24, 23, 23 called at the same instant give IDs 232, 244, 237, 239 - not monotonically increasing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: get_id on m2 -> 232 get_id on m4 -> 244 get_id on m7 -> 237 get_id on m9 -> 239 Not monotonically increasing

statement: Instead of keeping ID generation in the application logic, create a central ID service; this should solve the clock skew problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Instead of keeping ID generation logic on the application logic, let's create a central ID service .... should solve the clock skew problem

statement: At this point the problem stops being ID generation and becomes clock synchronization.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * Instead of thinking about ID generation, we are talking Clock Synchronization

statement: Central ID generation service: clients call one ID server, which runs the same get_id function to generate monotonically increasing IDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Central ID generation service We run the same get_id function in ID server to generate monotonically increasing IDs

statement: The central ID service is a single point of failure: the ID server or its disk could fail.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But, this central ID service is a SPoF ! ID server could fail Disk of the server could fail

statement: To solve the SPoF, add multiple ID servers behind a load balancer; these servers must gossip to converge on an agreed value.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: To solve SPoF, we add multiple ID servers behind a load balancer These ID servers need to gossip to converge upon an agreed value.

statement: Adding replicated, gossiping ID servers makes the whole process super complicated.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We made the entire process super complicakd !!

statement: Lesson: there is no way to distribute ID generation and guarantee strict monotonicity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One thing we did learn from these evolutions is that There is no way to distribute and guarantee strict monotonicity

statement: So real-world solutions relax constraints: non-integer IDs or no monotonicity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, the solutions we see out there have relaxed constraints -> Non- Integer IDs -> No monotonicity

speaker: teacher
verbatim: Central ID service with Batching : Amazon's Way

statement: The ID service keeps a table of counters per service (orders, payments); a batch request advances the service's counter by the batch size.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Service | counter orders 0 500 1000 payments 0 2000

detail: Drawn: light-blue box with a pink cylinder, stacked API boxes and a load-balancer bar.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: APIs for ID Svc

verbatim: Anytime a server of a service wants IDs, it makes a call to ID generation service and asks for a batch (500,1000, etc) it ...

speaker: teacher
verbatim: orders : server 1 : get_id_batch (500) orders : server 2 : get_id_batch (1000) payments : server 1 : get_id_batch (2000)

statement: Why build ID generation if UUIDs exist: UUIDs are 128-bit integers and very inefficient at scale - they do not index well and bloat the index.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why are we building ID generation, if UUID already exists ? UUIDs are 128 bit integers and are very inefficient at scale, - they ...

statement: UUIDs are random, which is good for security.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: + they are random - good for security

statement: A 4-byte int vs a 16-byte UUID makes indexes 4x larger; index lookups become disk I/O, so DB performance takes a hit.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 4 byte int v/s 16 byte int Your indexes are 4x larger. Your index lookups are disk I/O So, DB performance takes a hit

statement: Flickr needed its own ID generation because its database was sharded: to avoid collisions and guarantee uniqueness.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why flickr needed its own ID generation ? - Database was sharded - To avoid collision & guarantee uniqueness

statement: Flickr did not use UUIDs because they index badly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why not UUIDs ? Because they index badly

statement: If you cannot fit the indexes in memory, you cannot make your DB fast.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you cannot fit the indexes in-memory, you cannot make your DB fast

statement: Database ticket server (Flickr): a central MySQL ticket server; whoever wants an ID fires a query to this DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Database Ticket Servers : Flickr Central Ticket Server: MySQL - whoever wants an ID, fires a query to this DB

statement: Ticket table: id bigint unsigned not null auto-increment (primary key) and stub char not null default '' (unique key); one row with a dummy stub value 'a'.

statement: Idea: deleting and re-inserting the row makes the DB generate the next auto-incremented id, which you use for your use case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Idea: Delek and re-insert the row will make DB generak the next id (autoincremenkd) Use this ID for your use case

statement: DELETE then INSERT in one transaction works but is extremely costly on the DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We can either DELETE and then INSERT in one transaction but it is extremely costly on the DB

statement: Upsert = delete + insert; MySQL provides two ways of doing it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: UPSERTS (Delete + Insert = Upsert) MySQL provides 2 ways of doing it

statement: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE tries to insert; if it fails due to a UNIQUE KEY, the update clause is executed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: INSERT ....... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE ....... tries to insert, if it fails due to UNIQUE KEY then the update clause is execukd

statement: REPLACE INTO tries to insert; if it fails due to a UNIQUE KEY, the old row is deleted and the new row inserted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: REPLACE INTO ..... tries to insert, if it fails due to UNIQUE KEY then the old row is delekd and the new row is inserkd.

statement: REPLACE INTO is 32x slower than ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: REPLACE INTO ..... ← This is 32x slower than ON DUPLICATE..

statement: Both upsert forms are atomic (compare upsert in a KV store).

statement: Snowflake (Twitter) is used for the IDs of tweets and was also adopted at Discord and Instagram.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Snowflake: Twitter Used for IDs of Tweets -> also adopkd at Discord and Instagram

statement: Snowflake IDs are 64-bit integers: 41 bits epoch millis, 10 bits machine ID, 12 bits counter (per machine).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Snowflakes are 64 bits integers 41 | 10 | 12 epoch millis machine ID counter (per machine)

statement: Snowflake puts time on the LHS and the tie breaker on the right.
detail: 'right' is cut off by the tiles.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * time on the LHS * tie breaker on the ri..

statement: Snowflake is not a central service; it runs in the app (API) servers as a native function, and the ID is computed while storing the tweet in the DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Snowflake is not a central service, instead it runs in app servers as a native function while storing the tweet in DB ID is computer

statement: Snowflakes are roughly sortable: the first 41 bits are epoch milliseconds, so with every ms the ID moves forward.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Snowflakes are Roughly Sortable First 41 bits are epoch milliseconds with every ms the ID will be moving forward

statement: Time-ordered IDs let you fetch objects before/after a certain time or before/after a certain ID, which is great for pagination.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This gives us an ability to get objects before/after a certain time before/after a certain ID Hence, pretty awesome for pagination

statement: Twitter's pagination is not limit/offset based; it uses since_id ('I read till this tweet, give me the next set').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Twitter's pagination is not limit/offset based, instead it uses 'since_id' to paginakd -> I read till this tweet, give me the next set

statement: This ID-based pagination is also used by sharded DBs like DDB and is extremely efficient.

verbatim: This type of pagination is also used by sharded DB like DDB and is extremely efficient
